selected.title: UK Businesses File £700m CAT Claim over Visa and Mastercard EEA Fees
selected.summary: A Competition Appeal Tribunal claim alleges the card networks raised UK-EEA interchange fees five-fold after Brexit, costing businesses up to £200m a year. The post UK Businesses File £700m CAT Claim over Visa and Mastercard EEA Fees appeared first on The Fintech Times .
selected.why: Major £700m antitrust claim filed against card networks over cross-border interchange fees.
selected.fullText: UK Businesses File £700m CAT Claim over Visa and Mastercard EEA Fees | The Fintech Times Facebook Twitter Instagram Linkedin Youtube About Editorial Calendar Contact Us Advertise Jobs Search for: Search Primary Menu Search for: Search Home World-Region-Country Europe UK Businesses File £700m CAT Claim over Visa and Mastercard EEA Fees Europe Paytech UK Businesses File £700m CAT Claim over Visa and Mastercard EEA Fees by The Fintech Times October 17, 2026 October 15, 2026 A collective proceedings claim worth more than £700 million has been filed against Visa and Mastercard at the UK Competition Appeal Tribunal, alleging the two card networks exploited the removal of EU interchange caps following Brexit to levy unlawful inter-regional fees on UK businesses accepting online payments from European Economic Area customers. The claim is brought by Ann Pope , a former Senior Director for Antitrust at the Competition and Markets Authority , acting through her vehicle Ann Pope Collective Proceedings Limited and represented by pan-European competition law firm Geradin Partners . The proposed class covers approximately 126,000 UK businesses that accepted remote payments from EEA-issued cards at any point since October 2020. Inclusion in the action is opt-out rather than opt-in, meaning businesses are automatically enrolled unless they choose to withdraw. The fee increase at the centre of the claim Before the end of the Brexit transition period, inter-regional interchange fees were subject to EU caps. After those caps ceased to apply to UK businesses, the Payment Systems Regulator found that Visa raised its UK-EEA online transaction fee five-fold in October 2021, moving from 0.2% to 1.15% for consumer debit cards and from 0.3% to 1.5% for consumer credit cards. Mastercard followed in April 2022 with equivalent increases. The claim argues this was not a legitimate commercial response to changed market conditions. The UK remained part of the Single Euro Payments Area after Brexit, meaning the underlying cost structure of processing EEA-issued card transactions did not change materially. The PSR has itself concluded that Visa and Mastercard faced no effective competitive constraints on the acquiring side of their networks when setting these fees, and has proposed a price cap that remains under active consideration but has not yet been implemented. reason: UK businesses filing £700m claim against Visa/Mastercard for post-Brexit fee rises creates genuine debate about whether network fee-setting powers need structural limits or whether market solutions suffice.
angle: Interchange fee regulation should address the structural problem of network gatekeeping power, not just cap individual decisions post-facto.
